question: A facilities manager used Claude with web search on and received an answer citing a national standard for emergency lighting inspection intervals. She plans to rewrite the depot inspection schedule around that interval. What should she do first?
options: A) Open the source that Claude cited and read what the standard itself says about intervals.
B) Search for other online articles that happen to mention the same inspection interval.
C) Apply the new interval at one depot first and see whether any problem shows up there.
D) Ask Claude to confirm that the interval it has given her is correct before she relies on it.
correct_answers: A) Open the source that Claude cited and read what the standard itself says about intervals.
explanations: Correct. Where web search produced the answer, reviewing the cited source is the recommended check, because reading the original reveals anything Claude has misinterpreted. With a safety-related schedule at stake, the standard's own wording is what she needs.

Secondary articles may all be repeating the same misreading, and agreement between them proves nothing about what the standard requires. The cited source is closer to the truth than any commentary on it.
Piloting a safety interval treats real depots as the test, and a lengthened interval would show its consequences only when something goes wrong. Reversibility is low here, so this is the wrong order.
Claude confirming its own claim adds confidence without adding evidence. Self-confirmation is not verification, and the citation offers a much stronger check that costs no more effort.
